[h1]In-Depth Analysis[/h1]
[h3]Pros[/h3]
[b]1.[/b]
Not only OMD2 stays on the course outlined by its predecessor, but manages to overhaul, refine and improve pretty much every aspect that made the series a success. Enemy variety, loadout choices, map complexity, challenge - on all this and more, the second chapter doubles down. The addition of full co-op mode in all levels is the crown jewel, that takes this title to another level.

[b]2.[/b]
Nightmare mode, unlocked only after completing the game on War Mage, isn't just the "regular" difficulty that makes enemies spongier or more numerous. Instead, it adds a bouquet of unique, never-seen-before foes such as the mighty Mountain Troll or the insidious Gnoll Grenadier, to name some. Playing levels on this setting will force players to re-define strategies, as the challenge cranks up significantly.

[b]3.[/b]
Each completed stage will unlock at least one new piece of equipment to buy at the shop, using Skulls (currency gained by completing levels). The variety of equipment and traps is really great, as they cater to all kinds of strategies or playstyles: one can choose to build a utility-focused character, or instead a purely offensive one, that relies on its own firepower more than anything else. Experimenting (and failing sometimes) with new builds is exciting.

[b]4.[/b]
The owners of the original game will be rewarded with some skins and additional content, other than ten levels straight from OMD1, remastered to accommodate the second chapter's gameplay overhauls, and co-op. Definitely a juicy addition.

[h3]Cons[/h3]
[b]1.[/b]
OMD2 still is plagued by the annoying time-based rating system, which rewards players for completing a level under a certain PAR time. Doing so is necessary to achieve 5 Skulls, the highest rating. The problem with this choice, is that enemy waves CANNOT be called-in early, in exchange for more challenge (as seen in many other Tower Defense), so this requirement is ultimately a bad design choice.

[b]2.[/b]
Nightmare is tough (and rightly so), however it shows more than anything else, how some levels were designed with two players in mind, especially those towards the latter pats of the campaign. There will be situations in which the lack of a second player really takes its toll, as only one simply won't be able to be in all places needing their support at the right time.

[b]3.[/b]
The hardest setting removes the strategical breaks every couple waves, seen in War Mage difficulty and below. These  "pause times" are crucial to re-organize defenses, as Tower Defense games are ultimately about strategy rather than quick reflexes. Removing them, thus forcing players to rush all the time, kinda goes against the nature of the TD genre entirely.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2457285443

[h1]Gameplay Breakdown[/h1]

[b]Equipment Management[/b]
Is performed at the beginning of each level, by selecting the defenses, weapons and trinkets one intends to carry with them in that stage. A limited number of slots is available, and the loadout can't be changed again, so choosing wisely is always the critical matter. After completing a level, the Spellbook panel allows upgrading existing tools or buying new ones using Skulls, a currency earned after each level. The better the performance (no core damage, no deaths, PAR time beaten...), the more skulls are earned each time.

[b]Preparation[/b]
Is done at the start, when players always have unlimited time to plan their initial defense, by placing traps that cost currency to be deployed. There isn't a hard limit to placed traps, but there is one for Guardians, which are AI-controlled minions like Archers - the limit is only defined by running out of cash. In-between waves, a small frame of ten seconds is given for quick sales or repairs, however defenses can be placed at ANY time, even during the heat of battle. As levels progress, new Doors that deploy enemies will open, often from multiple directions, so rebalancing, transferring and weighing each side of one's defensive perimeter is an ever-evolving task. 

[b]Combat[/b]
Plays out in a third-person shooter fashion, with players able of using a wide array of ranged and melee weapons to suit all tastes. Some of such tools use Mana, which slowly recharges over time, while others have unlimited, free-to-use attacks. Different elements from both traps and weapons may be better suited for specific enemies: for example, a Frost Ogre will be highly vulnerable to fire, so accounting for this is an important part of the combat strategy.

If the player is killed, some points will be subtracted to the Rift (core)'s health, immediately forfeiting an eventual Perfect "5 Skulls" rating. Better watch out, as most enemies, especially heavy ones, may very well kill players in just a few hits, and also stun / debuff them. Traps cannot be damaged or disabled in any way by enemies, however some of them already present in the level's layout, may be one-time use only (like the devastating Rolling Log). 

All traps reload automatically after a set time, and fire again as soon as an enemy enters their kill-zone. Instead, Guardians (minions) can be killed in action, but also resuscitate every couple waves, or immediately if players have a specific item that allows it. Generally, the combination of player support and trap placement is key to win a match. Combining many effects of traps, trinkets and elements generates Combo Kills, which result in massively boosted currency gains - which are vital.

Orcs Must Die! 2 is the follow up to Orcs Must Die 1, and is a third person tower defence game, developed by Robot Entertainment.  The game was released on PC July 2012. 

The main difference with Orcs Must Die 2 is the addition of co-op gameplay. Everything else is virtually the same. You play either as a War Mage or sorceress in the story mode. You have to defend at one or more rifts which open at the start of the level. Each level has a varying amount of waves of enemies continuously spawning in order to reach said rift. Your aim is to stop them by building traps whilst also using your own character to kill them as well. Before each level you choose your load out of traps that you want to use. You start out by only being able to take 4 or 5, but work your way up to being able to take 10 traps on a stage with you.  Before jumping into each level too, you can upgrade your traps to do more damage, have a lower cool down time, or some other ability such as slowing the enemy if they are hit by it for example.  You'll notice from the very beginning that there are a few traps that you'll always want to take with you, such as the slowing trap - but included in your loadout, is your characters weapon, so you have to choose carefully. 

You are given an infinite amount of time to build your traps at the start of each level, and you are also given a healthy amount of time between waves to allow you to build more. You are granted extra coins after each wave, and for killing enemies, and you use these coins to purchase more traps. Whilst you can also place traps when enemies are spawning, this isn't always a good idea as your main focus should be on killing enemies then.  A large portion of this game is actually you spamming your left mouse button using your main weapon, whilst you aren't able to destroy everything with this weapon; it is more used as filler for your time as most of the damage will come from the traps.  There is a huge variety of traps as well, and you probably won't even use them all even by the end of the game, leaving you plenty of chances to experiment. 

The graphics in Orcs Must Die 2 are really nice. They are in the cartoon style that many of us really enjoy, but they aren't so childish that they can't portray the maturity of the title. There are some really nice special effects, such as the lava and ice traps, they all look marvellous. Everything is perfectly animated too, whilst a lot of the enemies are copy/pasted, that is to be expected from a game of this type.

Orcs Must Die 2 has a very catchy sound track too; the song is played constantly and it will be driven into your head and you'll be whistling it without realising it. Other than the soundtrack, the rest of the game's audio is brilliant too. The game is narrated in the cut scenes by the male character; it would have been nice to get voice acting on the female though. 

This game has varying levels of difficulty, the regular easy, medium and hard mode. You only unlock hard mode after you have beaten the game. There is one other form of difficulty, and that is endless mode. This will pit you against an endless stream of enemies, meaning you have to constantly upgrade your traps and the enemies will not stop until they either kill you or destroy your rift. This mode will really test your metal but is extremely fun to play in. Most players should really be playing this game on the Medium skill level, the easy mode is too easy and will not really offer any challenge to any tower defence veteran. 

All of the levels in Orcs Must Die 2 are so well designed; I cannot find any faults with them at all. The early stages of the game are a tutorial stage really, allowing you to test out your traps to work out how they are best used, so the levels are pretty simple, but once you reach the end levels, you'll really be putting your trap building skills to the test, as you have to defend multiple rifts from multiple entry points of enemies. Some of the bigger levels offer a bit of support in getting around quickly in the form of teleporters, these will teleport you to the other side of the map once stepping in them. 

I have been playing Orcs Must Die 2 for almost thirty hours, this is because there is absolutely tons of content in this game, not only is the single player story mode eight hours of gameplay, you also have the added replay ability of playing the story again as the other hero (with different skills and abilities), and then you also can replay the whole game again on co-op which adds a whole another level of content as the enemies are all scaled up to match you and your friend - and finally, we have the endless mode, this is the part of the game that I have spent the majority of my time and I am absolutely hooked on it. As you play the story mode, once you reach the final waves of a level, you'll often feel like you wish you could carry on and see how far you get, you can do that in endless mode; you just keep building traps, and facing more and more enemies as they just keep coming. This mode alone has given me about fifteen hours of gameplay. 

Orcs Must Die 2 can be played on all resolutions. I played on 4k with everything on max settings and was able to get 60 FPS constantly. I did however have a few crashes, this mainly happened when you minimize the game too many times, and it gives you a message something regarding DirectX. Although this was annoying, I only had it when minimizing and not whilst in the midst of gameplay. The game can be played with a controller, but as it has elements of aiming with a crosshairs, the game is highly recommended to be played with a keyboard/mouse - it just works so much better on them. 

This game is an absolute must play for any tower defence fan, if you had any sort of enjoyment out of the first, you'll get more of the same out of this, and the added edition of co-op makes it even more appealing to a wider audience. Not to mention the hours and hours of content on offer in this game. The regular price tag of £10, 99 is fairly marked and should be considered a must play for me.

Greetings Again!  After beating the original OMD I decided to move immediately to the sequel which is what we have here.  In my opinion this game improves on the original in every way; no we don’t see a graphics update but primarily an update to the mechanics and design.

Even more Orcs:  Not only do we have more types of orcs but also other types of enemies; some of which fundamentally change the way you have to play.  Of course the trap types have improved and you are given a much more in depth advancement system in the ways of spending skulls to improve traps in 3 to 4 ways.  Generally, the first option is just making it more effective but some of the secondary options change the way the traps can be used (such as putting them on ceilings or adding poison).

Crazy Lady Playtime:    In addition to all the improvements the game includes one that I felt was sorely needed; namely co-op.  This also comes with a new character; the sorceress from the first game who actually has some traps and equipment that is unique to her.  Both characters are playable but mechanically I prefer the war mage over the sorceress.  Other than that you get all of the typical things such as leader boards but the main bonus here is co-op.

I’m the Greatest:  The game is great; no doubt about that and definitely an improvement but I try to always level a few areas that I think can be improved upon.  In my time replaying the game I had several crashes; usually at the end of the level (making it even more frustrating); the game usually recorded the win but I ended up having to replay the level in case there was some story I missed.  This happened on the final mission as well which was kind of annoying.  Another improvement is that I’d like some kind of checkpoint or saving option.  Maybe this isn’t needed if I didn’t have to worry about crashing.  I also would have liked some more dynamic levels; especially those that required co-op or those that focused around a specific technique; maybe levels that prevented the use of certain items.

Overall, I still love the game and definitely worth every penny sale or not.  There is some DLC and it is worth a buy but overall I felt a bit meh about it.  I’m a sucker for more storyline (which there is none) and more content but didn’t really grab me like the original game.  Regardless; I’d still recommend the DLC as well.  Enjoy!

Using a wide range of abilities and traps, you must stop a horde of orcs and related beasties from traversing a dungeon and making their way to your sacred portal.

For those of you who have never played [i]Orcs Must Die![/i], it is a tower defense game that allows the player to freely roam the environment. You’ll be allowed to pre-pick what traps and weapons you’d like to use before the waves of enemies start coming, place said traps, and then take an active role in stopping them yourself. 

The gameplay is a mixture between classic tower defense and third-person action, and as you play through the campaign you unlock increasingly more powerful traps and weapons. It’s a pretty straightforward premise, but the end result is something which is surprisingly compelling and challenging.

One big addition is the cooperative mode, which many felt was sorely missing from the first game. If you enjoyed [i]Orcs Must Die![/i] on your own, then you can roughly double your expected enjoyment factor when playing [b][i]Orcs Must Die! 2[/i][/b] with a friend

All in all, [b][i]Orcs Must Die! 2[/i][/b] is a great game. And if you liked [i]Orcs Must Die![/i] or just enjoy a good tower defense game, then give this game your attention.

I enjoyed the first Orcs Must Die! and I enjoyed this one too. I would strongly recommend this game to just about anyone. Even if you're a bit unsure about getting Orcs Must Die!, you should definitely try Orcs Must Die! 2. It fixes many of the cons of the original game, so here's a list of pros and cons.

PROS
-Great and easy to learn gameplay.
-Two unique characters with arsenals varying enough to effect gameplay while not have too much difference between them.
-Improved graphics from the original game.
-Funny dialogue and commentary that serves both the entertainment value of the game and the story aspects of the game (which is surprisingly satisfying given how little there actually is).
-Unlike its predecessor, there's multiplayer (albeit only dual multiplayer). And, even better, it makes sense in the story's context.
-Tweaks the traps and weapons from the original game to balance them more.
-Has great DLC that you should definitely try out.
-Much more dynamic currency system (concerning the skulls) than the original game.
-Keeps the Nightmare difficulty and adds the new Endless levels.
-Expands the player's equipment to include trinkets and cosmetics.

CONS
-Multiplayer is limited to two people. Not a con for me personally, but it might be for some.
-Tweaks the traps and weapons from the original game. Again, not a con for me personally, but I have heard some complaints concerning some of the changes.
-DLC costs money. Depending on who you are, this might be a con. I personally didn't mind. The DLC was great.

So, yeah, that's it. Not much do I have to complain about, and though I am sure other pros and cons exist, I can't think of them off the top of my head. Regardless, though, I highly recommend trying out this game. Odds are, it'll be a blast.

When you play Orcs Must Die! 2 alone, you notice something almost immediately; the design of the new levels is clearly built for Co-Op action with a friend. Most of the time through barricades or planning you could get 3 or 4 doors worth of orcs to run through one setup of traps, which is about what was needed to clear the levels on War Mage difficulty. Sadly, about midway through OMD!2, it seems someone decided to make a whole pile of symmetrical levels in which there is no common area to filter all of the orcs through. Fair enough, it must still be possible to do it alone right?

If you've played the first game, you can picture what I am going to describe now: Imagine a 6 square wide path. There is only a buildable wall on one side. The other side of the path has a few blocks of lava, which cannot be used because if you try to throw them into it they just fly clear of the lava river onto the symmetrical path on the other side (past the point where your traps would be). There is a small section with a ceiling on which to build ceiling traps but Swinging Mace now basically does no damage and just throws the orcs away from your other traps. If you spend all of your money on one side of the level, you might get lucky with a setup that can stop the first 2 waves using all of the right traps in the limited possible building areas, but what do you do on the other side? Fight the whole waves yourself with no trap assistance? Goodluck, it works for a few levels and then you just get completely overwhelmed, You never end up with enough money to defend both sides, and you need to spend what you get to build up your untrapped side, and the original side that you built to start is leaking orcs (a lot of them) every level.

There are a few levels like this in a row probably about 75% of the way through the game. You clearly need 2 players, so each can play their own separate game on their own side of the level. How is that fun?

With OMD 1 and its mini expansion I spent about 8 hours on the medium difficulty. I had to restart some levels, readjust strategy, etc. But overall, the levels were pretty fair and you got around via portals quickly. In OMD 2 this has been - for the most part - completely scrapped. Pretty much every map has been specifically designed around 2 player co-op. From what I've heard, later levels are supposedly next to impossible on higher difficulties. The DLC packs are "a bit" better in that regard, but suffer from the same problems. This also results in later levels not being able to complete the "par times" for a map, which in turn results in less skulls, which in turn means you have to play more to earn enough to unlock new stuff or upgrade existing stuff. And due to the map layouts it's almost impossible to cover all "lanes" and build new traps, because you only have 10 seconds between each wave on normal, until you get a respite every 3 or so levels, but then again, it takes so much time just to MOVE to the other side of the map that you can't keep under par. Even on easy I'm like 4-5 minutes above them at times. Never had a problem in OMD 1 on normal 0o. More on that later. I think the maps are fine for co-op, but if you just want to murder some Orcs, stick to OMD 1. (Apparently Orcs Unchained is even worse).

Unlocks: In OMD 1 you got a new trap after every level you beat in the campaign. That system wasn't flawless, but it kept you going. In OMD 2 I unlocked not a whole lot by playing, but by paying instead. You get skulls for beating a level (up to 5) and bonus skulls for...I don't even know. Sometimes enemies drop them. Maybe it's for achievements like total number of career kills or something. While you can get a lot of skulls early on, obviously it becomes more difficult later and the unlocks themselves are very expensive, since there are 3 tiers for each trap + a special ability to unlock (that was 1 unlock in OMD 1, albeit a more expensive upfront cost). Since there are no damage numbers in the game, you can't even verify what the improvement is. Most higher level traps also have to be unlocked via skulls in the first place (I'd say more than half of the traps available in the game). The only good part about it is that you can refund all of your skulls at any given point and are able to redistribute them. Your lovely idiot from the first game is now being accompanied by the "evil" female apprentice. The idiot however starts not with his trusty crossbow for some reason (which can be unlocked for skulls, but is totally pointless, since it deals less damage, has less stopping power and is so terribly inaccurate that it hurts compared to his main weapon), but with a shotgun. The pro, however, is that it can be upgraded to knock over most heavy monsters. [h1][u][b]About Orcs Must Die! 2:[/b][/u][/h1]
It is a fast paced, tower defense game which requires you to be crafty and resourceful from the beginning until the end. But unlike most common defense tower games you actively participate in the battle, you are main defense, your towers, or rather traps, will hinder, soften or thin out the horde, but you'll still have a lot of heavy lifting to do by yourself.

[h1][u][b]About the gameplay[/b][/u][/h1]
Orcs Must Die! 2 is more refined than its predecessor, it fixes little tweaks that were very annoying in the first game and balances weapons that back then felt a little too powerful and buffs weapons that were otherwise almost useless or felt too weak to be of proper use.

There's a lot of variation in your towers, or rather, traps. You can out them on the ground, walls and ceiling and some traps requires certain strategies to work well. Obviously there are traps that works better with others, but nothing is truly impossible to combine, you create your own set of traps to watch enemies get brutally pierced/crushed/burnt/frozen/stripped to the bones.

The game makes sure to bring new foes and tricks to ensure that you will always try something new, something you hadn't thought before or to show that your old tactics will eventually stop working. 

[h1][u][b]Improvements over the first game[/b][/u][/h1]
Orcs Must Die! 2 fixes a lot of little things that were annoying in the first game some are noticeable such as clunky physics with Wind Belt, other are more subtle like not being able to place Boom Barrels too close to enemies and removing fall damage which was completely needless.

Another big change was the improvements over control customization and options overall which was seriously lacking in the first Orcs Must Die!

All in all once you play the first game you'll realize how the differences can affect in your game style.

[h1][u][b]How difficulty is it?[/b][/u][/h1]
Orcs Must Die! 2 can be difficult, a bit overwhelming at first, but you will rarely feel that the game was unfair, that it did something ridiculous that you couldn't counter before it happened. It is a rewarding experience and you will feel great whenever you pull a maximum rank victory, especially on Nightmare (I'll talk about it in a moment).

The game was tailored for co-op action and after the first stage you'll be facing two enemy spawn points to defend and it can feel unfair, especially in the beginning when you barely have anything to deal with them, it can be difficult but it's still manageable.

While not something I truly appreciate, you'll have to go back to certain levels when you have better equipment to ace it (5 skull). Sure, you can start playing from the get go with a friend, but damn if it doesn't make you feel like a complete pro player when you get that maximum rank victory in a difficult map all by yourself.

[h1][u][b]Nightmare?[/b][/u][/h1]
The Nightmare difficulty, unlocked by finishing the game once, is far from being a numerical difficulty where the game merely ups enemies health or their numbers (something that plagues the games ever since they were made), it ramps up the difficulty to above the roof showing even tougher enemies and giving you puny three seconds to sell traps/units. You'll be forced to rethink your strategies and sometimes change to things you never ever thought before.

[h1][u][b]Bring friend to kill orcs. Have twice as fun.[/b][/u][/h1]
The co-op is just plain fun. Even more enemies to kill with a friend is never enough and being able to share strategies and putting up your traps into synergy is pure glee. If you don't have friends to play with you can always ask for others in the multiplayer groups.

[h1][u][b]Orcs Must Die, sure, but there are few problems...[/b][/u][/h1]
There are two complaints about this great game I have: grinding and character selection.
Grinding is bad enough (maximizing traps, accessories and weapons is expensive), but having to do twice because you have to create two separate game files for each character is just increasing the longevity of the game in a bad way, especially since it can take a while to notice the differences between both characters aside from the obvious.

Changing characters requires you to return to the main menu screen, which wouldn't be such a hassle if you didn't have to leave the Party you made for multiplayer which can be very annoying.

There's also the fact Orcs Must Die! 2 is MUCH shorter than it's predecessor. While the first game has whooping 24 maps in the main campaign, the second game has only 15. Of course with the Classic levels DLC (earned by having the first game) the second game is longer, but I'm was never a big fan of having to rely on DLC to have a game with good length.

[h1][u][b]Final commentaries[/b][/u][/h1]
Orcs Must Die! 2 is an excellent game. It has tons of replay value and is balanced decently for both co-op and solo play. It does feel like it's an "Orcs Must Die! 1 v2.0" but with so many new traps, a new character and a good amount of changes, fixes here and there, it's worth every penny.

Even after the release of Orcs Must Die! 3 this game holds up very well and it stands being the best in the admittedly niche the Tower Defense genre is.

[b]Orcs Must Die! 2[/b] does a great job taking 3rd-person action elements and blending them with some tower defense to establish a good basis. It’s definitely the kind of game you can dive right into and get hooked for hours. 

There is a relatively large amount of different towers and abilities in the game when compared to many other games in the tower defense genre. You have plenty of options and can have fun experimenting with different strategies. The level designs also vary enough that they call for different approaches to beat them, so you will have to try out different tactics in order to succeed. And there is a fair amount of different enemies which keeps things fresh as you progress through the game.

There is also a scoring system and leaderboards to add replay value.

[b]Orcs Must Die! 2[/b] is a step forward from the already amazing first game.  All the good aspects return, with some new ideas sprinkled in. There are many more traps and abilities, and a more extensive upgrade system.  There are many new enemies.  There’s a new extensive campaign, new game modes (like endless mode), and with the Steam Workshop there are now limitless possibilities for maps.  

Also the addition of cooperative mode makes the experience exponentially more fun if you have a friend to play with.  

I would say practically everyone should enjoy the [i]Orcs Must Die![/i] games.  Many hours of fun to be had with the games in this series, I recommend playing both.

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world largely remains unchanged from OMD - there are various maps that serve as arenas for the tower defense. The maps do seem more varied here than just a simple castle-like environment, which is good. There is still no meaningful exploration or secrets to be found though. 

Continues the small narrative from the first game, but this time the antagonist joins the war mage as an optional 2nd character or co-op companion. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [7/10] [/b] [/h1]
It appears on the surface that the mechanics have been significantly improved, but there are some evident negatives that I found. 
The biggest improvement is the trap progression. I liked the upgrade system and how you can choose a specialization for each trap. Thankfully, with the improved trap progression, there’s also the ability to reset improvements. I sorely wish that I could simply remove improvements from a single trap instead of being forced to remove them from all traps. 
There’s also expanded items to slot. Aside from just traps, there’s a slew of new weapons, and even trinkets now which give you a passive effect. Very nice, but an unfortunate side effect is that your slots are now insanely valuable. With how the levels are set up and expanded for co-op, if you’re playing solo you really need to utilize every given slot for your traps, guardians, and now passive setups. 

This game can be exceptionally difficult, mostly due to the fact that this seems very heavily focused on co-op, so much so that you're going to have a rough time solo playing some of the levels. The later half of the story is frustratingly annoying as I constantly sprinted between 4 rooms trying to keep track of constantly flowing in orcs. This would have been much better with a 2nd person. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
Another massive improvement over OMD is not so much the graphics, but the technical side. 
Graphically, this is very slightly better than OMD, still around PS3-era. 
Technical side, while there still isn’t a lot of PC-focused options, there is a lot less bugs and issues with the UI and crashes. 
There were some bugs as well, but nothing like OMD, much better here.

Very similar audio as OMD, mostly having 2 variations of the music. 
There’s more voice acting over OMD, still good quality. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
Improved replay value here with more levels, endless mode, two different characters, each with their own traps, and of course co-op. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
Orcs Must Die! 2 (OMD2) brings the OMD series two steps forward, and one step back. Nearly every area of the game has had great improvements. Things like mechanics and technical aspects are much better. However, all the shiny new mechanics and technical parts can’t change the foundational design of the game being focused on a co-op experience. That means i you’re playing solo, like I was, then you may have a bad time. 

Like OMD2 does, I want to focus on the co-op aspects and how this impacts the game as a solo player. 
What becomes evident as you get further into the levels is how much of a pain it is to cover 4+ paths of orcs. Having another player would alleviate much of the stress between jumping constantly between lanes trying to stop orcs that got through your trap field. Even on the “Normal” difficulty of Warmage, its easy to get overwhelmed with trying to cover so many lanes. 
There’s also 2 different characters, each with their own traps. They tend to compliment each other, so by playing solo with one your missing out on some fundamental traps that the other has, like playing as the sorceress and not having the Tar trap is rough. 
All of these are major factors that a solo player should consider. You can definitely beat the game as solo, but when it comes to scoring high on the leaderboards or even just maxing the skulls for the levels, you’re going to have a tough time. 

Overall though, I believe that OMD2 has made net positive changes over OMD1 and thus this is easier to recommend as the better game.

I like this game so much that I kinda hate it now.  Well, maybe 'hate' is a strong word. We'll get to that later. Anyway, Orcs Must Die 2 is a fun and challenging tower defense game where you set up traps & mercenaries and use weapons & spells to keep an invading Orc army from breaking through the gates of your fortress.  The orcs are cartoonish and goofy (except for the hunters; they're cartoonish and awesome) and there are dozens and dozens of traps in your spell book that you can use to slow down or kill the orcs. You can only use 10 weapons/spells/traps/mercenaries/trinkets on each level though, so it may take a few run throughs to decide if, say, you should use decoys, barriers and archers, or acid baths, catapults and wall grinders. You start off with a set amount of gold coins that allows you to buy and place a limited amount of traps, and with every orc you kill you earn some more gold coins to buy and place more traps, either on the fly or between rounds. Each map has multiple rounds of increased difficulty with Round 1 comprising of a handful of slow moving and lightly armored little orcs up through the later rounds where more and more orcs of ever increasing strength and speed and abilities swarm the map.

Depending on how fast you vanquish the orcs and how many successfully penetrate your defenses over the course of all the rounds (I think they all have 9 rounds?), you can earn between 0 and 5 skulls to use to acquire more spells and traps for your spell book. It's a sliding scale. The longer it takes and/or the more that get through, the lower the number of skulls you get if you win. And if too many get through you lose. But if you kill 'em all quickly? 5 skulls for you!

The game can be played alone or in teams of two. It makes for a fun multiplayer experience as you coordinate with your teammate who will guard what areas and who will use what traps, along with updates on what areas are being overwhelmed and how each person is doing on health and mana.

So why the hate? Again, 'hate' is a strong word, but this game has can be pretty addicting. It has a leaderboard that keeps track of your highest score for each map and shows it in comparison to your friends as well as where your high score ranks with the high scores of everyone who's ever finished that map. I found myself obsessing over my score on the leaderboard on a few maps: "Which part should I set my traps in first? Which traps should I use? What if I swapped out the catapult for springing spikes?' etc. I'd play those maps over and over, trying to get a little faster and maximize the gold coins I earned on each kill. It... was unhealthy.

But that's a me problem, not a game problem. It's a great game and because it's so great that I found myself playing waaaay too much.

Orcs Must Die! was a tower defense puzzle game with arcade combat and horde fighting elements woven in.

Orcs Must Die! 2 is an arcade horde shooter with no puzzle aspect and barely any tower defense elements, since your traps don't do much and you're mostly just running around frantically shooting enemies.

If you like horde shooters, Earth Defense Force is better. If you like tower defense, OMD! 1 is the best of the genre, period.

But this game has nothing to do with the first one in terms of how to play it. The first one is about solving the puzzle of where to put traps and which ones to use, and shooting the horde down was how you shore up defenses and make your traps and guardians more effective.

In OMD! 2, your traps and guardians don't matter, only how effective your twitch shooting and sprinting skills are. There is no intellectual element whatsoever.
